James Gilmour
JAYMZ GIL-mor
proper noun
James from the Hebrew Ya’aqob through the Greek Iakōbos, “supplanter”; Gilmour a Scottish surname meaning “servant of Mary” in its Gaelic root; he was “Gilmour of Mongolia.”

Biblical Definition

James Gilmour (1843–1891) was a Scottish missionary to Mongolia, a lonely and largely fruitless labor borne with rare patience and self-denial for the love of Christ. Sent by the London Missionary Society to revive a long-dormant work among the Mongols, he set out from Peking onto the vast plains, learning the Mongolian tongue, adopting the dress and diet of the people, and traveling the steppe and desert with the nomads in their tents. Few missionaries have known so barren a field; he labored for years before he could count a single convert, and he buried his wife and children far from home. Yet he held on, an evangelist on horseback distributing Scriptures and tracts, doctoring the sick, and reasoning with lamas and herdsmen alike, returning again and again to a people slow to receive the word. He kept a journal of singular honesty, recording his loneliness and his unbroken trust in the God who had called him. He held the gospel to be the one hope of the Mongol multitudes bound in the darkness of Buddhism and superstition, and he counted the scarcity of fruit no reason to abandon the seed (1Co 3:6). He died at his post, worn out in the service of Christ. He stands among the most self-effacing laborers of the Great Commission, faithful where almost nothing visibly grew.

Webster 1828 Definition

A Scottish missionary to Mongolia who labored years among the nomads with little visible fruit, faithful to the end.

JAMES GILMOUR, a Scottish missionary to Mongolia (1843–1891) sent by the London Missionary Society.

He learned the Mongolian tongue and traveled the steppe and desert in the dress of the nomads.

He labored years before a single convert, and buried his wife and children on the field.

He went as an evangelist on horseback, distributing Scriptures and doctoring the sick.

He kept an honest journal of his loneliness and his unbroken trust in God, and died at his post.

Key Scripture

1Co 3:6 — "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase."

Gal 6:9 — "And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not."

Isa 55:11 — "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."

1Co 4:2 — "Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful."

Modern Corruption

Gilmour’s barren field is misread by a results-driven age that measures a mission only by its converts, and by anti-missions critics who scorn his labor among the nomads.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The distortion that most threatens Gilmour’s memory is the pragmatic creed of our day, which weighs a ministry only by visible numbers and would judge his decades among the Mongols a failure for want of converts. The Scripture forbids the verdict. Paul may plant and Apollos water, but God gives the increase (1Co 3:6); the steward is required only to be found faithful (1Co 4:2). Gilmour sowed the word that does not return void (Isa 55:11), and the fruit of such sowing is not always seen by the sower. To despise faithful labor that lacks a harvest is to despise the very pattern of the prophets and apostles.

The lesson to recover is that obedience, not visible success, is the measure of the laborer, and that we must not be weary in well doing, for in due season we shall reap if we faint not (Gal 6:9). Gilmour’s lonely steppe, his buried family, and his sparse fruit make him a rebuke to a church enamored of quick results and crowded altars. The God who sent him will not forget his work, and the seed he scattered upon those plains remains in the keeping of the One who gives the increase in His own time.

Hebrew Roots

A supplanter by name, he supplanted his own ease for the love of a forgotten people on the steppe.

expand to see more

James — from Hebrew Ya’aqob through Greek Iakōbos, “supplanter.”

Gilmour — a Scottish surname; in Gaelic root, “servant of Mary” or devotee.

He was known simply as “Gilmour of Mongolia,” bound to one hard field.

The verb that ruled his life was to plant, leaving the increase to God (1Co 3:6).

“Mongolia” named the vast steppe and desert where he sowed among the wandering tribes.

Usage

"James Gilmour rode the Mongolian steppe for years before he saw a single soul turn to Christ."

"Though loneliness pressed hard upon him, James Gilmour would not leave the field God gave him."

"James Gilmour planted the seed and trusted God for an increase he might never see."
